text: Τόμος δογματικός. Hunc magna parte sive librum, sive epistolam, Anastasius Bibliothecarius in sua Collectanea retulit, ea deflorans ac sublegens, quæ Honorii papæ defensionem contineant. Ac sane gratulandum tantum monumentum et cimelium in pontificia Romæ asservatum gaza, vel nunc demum qua productum est lingua, Gallicani cleri sedulitate et ope; inque eo splendidissimi surgentis jubaris, pari nobilitate, vita, doctrina, serenissimi principis ducis d'Abret Em. card. propensissima liberalitate, ac episcopi suprema arce Palatini, in lucem prodire: ut eo, ac reliquis Maximi, filia suppetias matri eat, arcemque vel maxime Romanam, quo tempore tantis turbinibus quatitur, fulciat, et sibi ipsa in ejus salute incolumitatem atque gloriam, avita in sedem apostolicam pietate, quærat. Nec una Honorii hic defensio, sed et Anastasii Sinaitæ, et Gregorii Theologi.
anchorLine: ΤΟΜΟΣ ΔΟΓΜΑΤΙΚΟΣ (x) ΠΡΟΣ ΜΑΡΙΝΟΝ ΠΡΕΣΒΥΤΕΡΟΝ.
en: "Τόμος δογματικός" (Dogmatic Tome). Anastasius the Librarian reported this work, whether a book or a letter, for the most part in his own Collectanea, culling and gleaning those parts which contain the defence of Pope Honorius. And indeed congratulation is due that so great a monument and treasure, kept in the pontifical store-house of Rome, has now at last been brought forth in the French language, through the diligence and aid of the Gallican clergy; and in it, by the most generous liberality of the most serene prince, Duke d'Abret, the Eminent Cardinal, with equal nobility, life and learning, a rising splendid light, and of the bishop, from the supreme Palatine citadel: so that by it and by the rest of Maximus's works, a daughter may come to the aid of her mother, and may support the Roman citadel above all, at a time when it is shaken by such great storms, and may seek for herself, in the Roman See's safety, security and glory, out of her ancestral piety toward the Apostolic See. Nor is this the sole defence of Honorius here, but also that of Anastasius the Sinaite and of Gregory the Theologian.

text: Τοῦ τῆς ἀναστάσεως φερωνύμως. Circumlocutio est, qua Anastasius Sinaita Antiochenus archiepiscopus Justino imperatore, describitur, libro adversus Joannem Philoponum; qui se fidei quasi indicem atque arbitrum, Catholicos inter et Severianos constituens, suæ illi lucubrationi Διαιτητὴν titulum fecerat, ut auctor est Nicephorus lib. xviii, c. 47, sive etiam περὶ ἑνώσεως, De unione. Lemmation ejus libri Anastasii refert Gretserus in Odegi proœmio, repertum inter adversaria Turriani. Ex quibus etiam τοῦ Διαιτητοῦ τεμάχιον, ex illius operis libro iv, pollicitus, cum quinque Anastasii orationes de rectis fidei dogmatibus editurus esset, fidem liberasse non videtur.
anchorLine: τοῦ τῆς ἀναστάσεως φερωνύμως (y) θειοτάτου καὶ
en: "Τοῦ τῆς ἀναστάσεως φερωνύμως" (of him who is rightly named from the Resurrection). It is a periphrasis by which Anastasius the Sinaite, archbishop of Antioch under the emperor Justin, is described, in the book against John Philoponus; who, setting himself up as a sort of judge and arbiter of the faith between the Catholics and the Severians, had given his own work the title 'Diaitetes' (the Arbiter), as Nicephorus attests, book 18, ch. 47, or also 'On Union', De unione. Gretser reports the heading of this book of Anastasius in the preface of the Hodegos, found among Turrianus's papers. Out of these he promised also a fragment of the Diaitetes, from book 4 of that work, when he was about to publish five orations of Anastasius on the right doctrines of the faith; he does not seem to have kept his promise.

text: Ὑπὲρ ἧς καὶ ἐξ ἧς ἑσπουδάσθη τῷ φιλοπόνῳ. Nempe Anastasio; quasi alludat ad ipsum adversarii nomen Φιλοπόνος · quo ipso Patres ægre eum indigitant, sæpiusque cum illis exciderit, velut emendando adjungunt, ἢ μᾶλλον ματαιοπόνος, ne sic ominato nominantes videantur aliquid indulgere Tritheitæ, aliisque erroribus nefasto hæretico. Paulo obscuriora videantur hæc Maximi, præsertim quod utriusque nos auctoris lucubratio deficiat; tum scilicet Anastasii pie hærentis menti Gregorii, nec tamen ea explicanda satis facilis, Philoponi depravantis, ac, si mavis, Matæoponi, non viri studiosi, sed hominis stulte laborantis.
anchorLine: λοπόνῳ (z), μικρὸν δὲ περὶ τὸ τῆς λέξεως ἀκριβὲς ἐν-
en: "Ὑπὲρ ἧς καὶ ἐξ ἧς ἑσπουδάσθη τῷ φιλοπόνῳ" (for which and from which the diligent one was zealous). Namely, for Anastasius; as though he were alluding to the very name of his adversary, Philoponos ("lover of toil"); the Fathers reproach him with this name with distress, and, since it fell out with them often, add as a correction, "or rather Mataiopónos" (vain-toiler), so that, by thus pronouncing a bad omen, they may not seem to indulge Tritheism or other errors with an ill-starred heretic. These words of Maximus may seem somewhat obscure, especially because the writing of both authors is lacking to us; on the one hand, because of Anastasius piously clinging to the mind of Gregory, yet not easy enough to explain, and on the other, of Philoponus, who distorts it, or, if you prefer, Matæoponus, not a man of study, but of one foolishly toiling.

text: Προσελήφθη ἡμετέρα φύσις, οὐχ ἁμαρτία. Sana hæc admodum, unaque forte Honorio, perinde ac Magno Athanasio, cogitata: nec tamen Macarius, quanquam Honorium sequi auctorem sibi videbatur, unamque illam ex Adæ culpa nobis inolitam, exscindere voluntatem, damnationem evasit; quod nempe homo dementissimus, sic abesse a Christo, ipsoque Adamo, vitium illud voluntatis humanæ contendebat, ut nec ipsa voluntas in eis humana esset, sed solum divina: quod certe in sani hominis mentem ne quidem venire possit, nec in Honorii, sapientissimi viri præstantissimique antistitis venisse putandum sit; nisi forte, eo duntaxat sensu, quod et humana, ipsa divina diceretur, quod ex divinis rationibus, et pro eo ac naturæ a Deo inditum erat a creatione moveretur; seu immobili rectitudine, ut in Christo ob unitionem, seu etiam in malum vertibili ex ipsa potestate arbitrii, ut in Adamo: quæ humanæ voluntatis non abolitio est, aut cum divina confusio; sed nativa, ut a Deo est, eique subjecta, illius perfectio. Paulo ante τὸ, συνδρομῆς, quod legit Anastasius, aptius est: et paulo post idem prope repetitur, ascripta Patri incarnationis effectione per Filium ac Spiritus cooperationem. Nihil bene Anastasius, jungendo τοῦ γένους cum ἡδονήν et reddendo generis desiderium; cum sit libido generi dominans (nobis scilicet ac mortalibus) a seductione.
anchorLine: ἐλήφθη ἡ ἡμετέρα φύσις, οὐχ ἁμαρτία (a)· » τουτ-
en: "Προσελήφθη ἡμετέρα φύσις, οὐχ ἁμαρτία" (our nature was assumed, not sin). These words are quite sound, and were perhaps conceived by Honorius just as by Athanasius the Great; yet Macarius, although he seemed to himself to follow Honorius as his authority, did not escape condemnation in cutting out that one will inherited by us from Adam's fault; for that most senseless man contended that it was so absent from Christ, and from Adam himself, the vice of the human will, that not even the human will itself was in them, but only the divine; which surely cannot enter the mind of a sane man, nor is it to be thought to have entered that of Honorius, a most wise man and most excellent prelate; unless perhaps in this sense alone, that the will would be called human, indeed divine, because it was moved from the divine reasons and, in accordance with what had been bestowed on nature by God, from creation; either with immovable rectitude, as in Christ by reason of the union, or also with a power of the will capable of turning to evil, as in Adam: which is not the abolition of the human will, nor its confusion with the divine, but a native will, as it is from God, and subject to him, the perfection of that will. A little before the word 'συνδρομῆς', which Anastasius read, is more apt; and a little later the same is almost repeated, the effecting of the Incarnation being ascribed to the Father through the Son and the co-operation of the Spirit. Anastasius is wrong in joining 'τοῦ γένους' with 'ἡδονήν' and rendering 'desire of the race', since the pleasure is a lust ruling over the race (that is, over us mortals), arising from seduction.

text: Πρὸς ὑποτύπωσιν ἡμῖν ἐκφαινόμενος. Ad nostram informationem elucens, ut nobis formula et exemplar esset: uti etiam Paulus II Tim. 1: Ὑποτύπωσιν ἔσχε ὑγιαινόντων λόγων, ὧν παρ' ἐμοῦ ἤκουσας: ubi Chrysost. metaphoram ait desumptam ex arte pictoria, qua pictores rem pingendam sibi delincant atque informant. Fulg., Formam habe sanorum verborum, quæ a me audisti. Anast. prorsus barbare, ad imaginationem nobis ostensa est; cujus et superiora, nullo sano sensu reddita; sed parcendum viro opera strenuo, sed non satis in Maximi stylo versato.
anchorLine: δείας δικαιοσύνης πρὸς ὑποτύπωσιν ἡμῖν ἐκφαινόμενος (b), καὶ τὸν ἐκ παραβάσεως ἐπεισαχθέντα τῇ
en: "Πρὸς ὑποτύπωσιν ἡμῖν ἐκφαινόμενος" (shining forth for our outline/pattern). Shining forth for our instruction, so that there might be a formula and example for us: as Paul too uses it in II Tim. 1: 'Ὑποτύπωσιν ἔσχε ὑγιαινόντων λόγων, ὧν παρ' ἐμοῦ ἤκουσας' (Hold the pattern of sound words which you heard from me); where Chrysostom says the metaphor is taken from the art of painting, in which painters outline and form for themselves the thing to be painted. Fulgentius: 'Hold the form of sound words which you have heard from me.' Anastasius: utterly barbarous: 'ad imaginationem nobis ostensa est' (was shown to us for the imagination); of which the earlier parts too are rendered without any sound sense; but one must spare a man diligent in his work, but not sufficiently versed in Maximus's style.
